title: Biggest Value on Each Level
statement:
Given the root of a binary tree, return a list with one number per level: the largest value on that level. The list goes from the root's level down to the deepest level.

An empty tree gives an empty list. Values can be negative.

examples.why: Level 0 is just 4. Level 1 holds 9 and 2. Level 2 holds 3, 8 and 6, and they come from different parents: the 8 under 2 beats the 3 under 9.
All values are negative. Starting each level's maximum at 0 would wrongly report 0 everywhere.

hints: You need to know which level every node is on. Which traversal visits the tree one level at a time?
Breadth-first search with a queue. At the start of each round, the queue holds exactly one level: remember its size and process that many nodes.
Start each level's maximum at the first node's value (or at −∞), never at 0. A depth-first walk also works if you pass the depth along and update result[depth].

explain.intuition:
This is a level-order walk with one number kept per level. A queue processed in rounds does it: when a round starts, the queue holds exactly the nodes of one level, so you take that many nodes out, track the largest value among them, and push their children for the next round.

A depth-first walk works too, as long as each call knows its depth. The first time you reach a new depth, append the node's value to the result; after that, take the maximum with result[depth]. Like reading a nested DOM tree and recording the widest element at each nesting depth.
steps: If the root is null, return an empty list.
Put the root in a queue.
While the queue is not empty, read its current size k. Take out k nodes, track the largest value, and push each node's non-null children.
Append that level's largest value to the result.
Return the result once the queue is empty.
pitfalls: Starting each level's maximum at 0. A level of all negative values would report 0.
Not freezing the level size before the inner loop. Children pushed during the round would be mixed into the current level.
Using recursion in a language with a small stack on a very deep tree. An explicit stack or the queue avoids it.

solutions.title: Depth-first with an explicit stack
solutions.idea: Carry the depth with each node. A new depth appends a value; a known depth takes the maximum.

solutions.title: Breadth-first, one level per round
solutions.idea: Process the queue in rounds of its current size; each round is one level, and its maximum is one answer.

followups: Return the leftmost value of each level instead. Which of the two walks makes that trivial?
Return the level with the largest sum. What changes in the queue version?
